title: Must, have to, don’t have to
goal: Talk about rules and what isn’t necessary
intro: “Must” and “have to” both mean something is necessary. “Must” often shows the speaker’s own feeling (“I must call Mom”), “have to” an outside rule (“I have to wear a uniform”). But in the negative they are very different: “mustn’t” means don’t do it, while “don’t have to” means it isn’t necessary.

rules.rule: must / have to + base form: it’s necessary.
examples: I have to be at work by nine.

rules.rule: don’t have to = it’s not necessary (you can if you want).
examples: She doesn’t have to work on Saturdays.
I had to wait for an hour.

mistakes.right: You must come. / You have to come.
mistakes.why: Use one: must OR have to.

mistakes.wrong: You mustn’t bring anything, we have food.
mistakes.right: You don’t have to bring anything.

mistakes.wrong: Yesterday I must go to the bank.
mistakes.right: Yesterday I had to go to the bank.

ex.q: You ___ wear a seatbelt. It’s the law.
It’s a holiday tomorrow, so I ___ get up early.
You ___ tell anyone. It’s a secret.
Last night we ___ take a taxi home.
My brother ___ travel a lot for work.
We must have to submit it today.
ex.fixed: We have to submit it today.

ex.q: Last week I must work on Sunday.
ex.fixed: Last week I had to work on Sunday.

ex.q: You mustn't pay now, you can pay later.
ex.fixed: You don't have to pay now, you can pay later.

ex.q: Does she ___ to wear a uniform?

ex.a: You don't have to reply today.

ex.q: Correct this: “We must have to finish this by Monday.”
a: We must finish this by Monday
We have to finish this by Monday
ex.y: Use one: must OR have to.

talk: Describe the rules at your office, college or home: what you have to do, what you mustn’t do, and what you don’t have to do.
